package.name: Sync
package.description: Locks, conditions, once-only initialization, semaphores, barriers, wait groups and channels for threads

modules.name: Channel
modules.header:
A queue that threads send values into and receive values out of, with room for a fixed number of them.
The values sit in a ring under one lock. A sender waits while the ring is full and a receiver while it is empty,
each on its own sequence word that the other side advances and wakes. Closing the channel wakes everyone: senders
then fail and get their value back, and receivers take what is left and then learn that nothing more will come.

modules.name: Counters
modules.header:
Coordination by counting: permits a semaphore hands out, threads a barrier waits for, and work a wait group waits
to see finished.
Each keeps its count in a word threads sleep on, and registers sleepers where waking them costs a system call, so
a release with nobody asleep is one atomic instruction.

modules.name: Lock
modules.header:
The two primitives that live where they are declared rather than in shared storage: a bare lock and a once-only
initialization. Neither needs destroying, so either can be a module variable, which every thread names directly,
or a field of a value that is itself shared.

modules.name: Mutex
modules.header:
A value that one thread at a time may reach, and the condition threads wait on while they hold it.
A `Mutex<T>` is a handle: the value and its lock live in storage every clone of the handle shares, so a thread is
given its own handle with `Clone` and the storage lasts until the last handle is gone. Locking returns a guard,
which is the only way to reach the value and which releases the lock when it is dropped.

modules.name: Native
modules.header:
Sleeping until a word in memory changes, and waking the threads that sleep on one: the one primitive every type in
this package is built from.
Each system checks the word in the kernel as it puts the thread to sleep, so a change that lands between a caller's
last look and its sleep ends the sleep at once rather than being missed. A sleep may also end for no reason the
caller can see, so every caller looks at the word again and decides whether to sleep once more.

modules.name: RwLock
modules.header:
A value many threads may read at once, or one thread may write.
The state word counts the readers holding the lock, or is `Writing` while a writer holds it. Waiters register in a
second word before they sleep, so a release only makes a system call when someone may be asleep; both words use
sequentially consistent operations, which is what keeps a release from missing a waiter that registered just
before it looked. Readers and writers are not queued in order, so a steady stream of readers can keep a writer
waiting.

modules.name: Word
modules.header:
The lock every type here takes, kept in one 32-bit word, and the counted storage the shareable types live in.
The word is 0 when the lock is free, 1 when it is held and nobody waits, and 2 when it is held and someone may be
sleeping on it. Taking a free lock and releasing one nobody waits for are each one atomic instruction; only a lock
that is actually contended costs a system call. A thread that has slept marks the word 2 when it takes the lock,
because it cannot know whether others still sleep, so the release after it wakes one.
The shareable types keep their state in a block allocated once and counted: every handle holds one count, and
whichever lets go of the last one destroys the block's contents and frees it.

doc.summary: A bounded queue of values passed between threads, any number of which may send and receive.
doc.markdown:
A bounded queue of values passed between threads, any number of which may send and receive.
Values arrive in the order they were sent. `Clone` gives another handle to the same channel; the values still in
it are destroyed when the last handle is gone. A handle is not copied.

doc.summary: A lock that guards nothing in particular: whatever the code between `Acquire` and `Release` touches.
doc.markdown:
A lock that guards nothing in particular: whatever the code between `Acquire` and `Release` touches.
Not reentrant: acquiring it again on the thread that holds it waits forever. Releasing it is the holder's job;
releasing a lock another thread holds, or one nobody holds, is a program error the lock cannot detect.
For data that a lock protects, `Mutex<T>` keeps the two together and releases the lock for you.

doc.summary: Runs one initialization once, however many threads ask for it at once.
doc.markdown:
Runs one initialization once, however many threads ask for it at once.
The first `Call` runs its function; every other waits until that has returned and then returns without running
its own. Everything the function wrote is visible to every thread `Call` returns on.

doc.summary: A condition threads wait on while holding a `Mutex<T>`, until another thread says it may hold.
doc.markdown:
A condition threads wait on while holding a `Mutex<T>`, until another thread says it may hold.
A wait releases the lock while it sleeps and takes it again before it returns, so the waiter re-checks the
condition under the lock. A wait may also return when nothing notified it, which is why it is always called in a
loop that checks the condition. `Clone` gives another handle to the same condition. A handle is not copied.
